claim: Understanding the variability of the environment is essential to function in everyday life.
source: Understanding the variability of the environment is essential to function in everyday life.
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance of understanding environmental variability, presented as established knowledge.

claim: The brain must take uncertainty into account when updating its internal model of the world.
source: The brain must hence take uncertainty into account when updating its internal model of the world.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim based on the premise about environmental variability and inference about brain function.

claim: Prediction errors arise from a difference between the current model and new sensory experiences.
source: The basis for updating the model are prediction errors that arise from a difference between the current model and new sensory experiences.
evidence: This is a definition based on established theoretical frameworks in neuroscience.

claim: Prediction error neurons have been identified in layer 2/3 of diverse brain areas.
source: Although prediction error neurons have been identified in layer 2/3 of diverse brain areas, how uncertainty modulates these errors and hence learning is, however, unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies throughout the manuscript.

claim: How uncertainty modulates prediction errors and learning is unclear.
source: Although prediction error neurons have been identified in layer 2/3 of diverse brain areas, how uncertainty modulates these errors and hence learning is, however, unclear.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Layer 2/3 neurons represent uncertainty-modulated prediction errors (UPE).
source: Here, we use a normative approach to derive how uncertainty should modulate prediction errors and postulate that layer 2/3 neurons represent uncertainty-modulated prediction errors (UPE).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their normative derivation.

claim: The layer 2/3 circuit calculates the UPE through subtractive and divisive inhibition by different inhibitory cell types.
source: We further hypothesise that the layer 2/3 circuit calculates the UPE through the subtractive and divisive inhibition by different inhibitory cell types.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors about circuit mechanisms.

claim: Different cell types can compute the means and variances of the stimulus distribution through local activity-dependent plasticity rules.
source: By implementing the calculation of UPEs in a microcircuit model, we show that different cell types can compute the means and variances of the stimulus distribution. With local activity-dependent plasticity rules, these computations can be learned context-dependently, and allow the prediction of upcoming stimuli and their distribution.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The mechanism enables an organism to optimise its learning strategy via adaptive learning rates.
source: Finally, the mechanism enables an organism to optimise its learning strategy via adaptive learning rates.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations shown in Figure 7.

claim: The brain maintains a model of the world based on which it can make predictions about upcoming stimuli.
source: Decades of cognitive research indicate that our brain maintains a model of the world, based on which it can make predictions about upcoming stimuli (Kveraga et al., 2007; Cohen et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Predicting sensory experience is useful for both perception and learning.
source: Predicting the sensory experience is useful for both perception and learning: Perception becomes more tolerant to uncertainty and noise when sensory information and predictions are integrated (Payzan-LeNestour and Bossaerts, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Humans estimate uncertainty and adjust their behaviour accordingly.
source: Behavioural and electrophysiological studies indicate that humans indeed estimate uncertainty and adjust their behaviour accordingly (Payzan-LeNestour and Bossaerts, 2011; Walker et al., 2019; Goris et al., 2018; Cannon et al., 2021; Körding and Wolpert, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to behavioral and electrophysiological studies.

claim: The activity of individual neurons of layer 2/3 cortical circuits in diverse cortical areas of mouse brains has been linked to prediction errors.
source: Recently, the activity of individual neurons of layer 2/3 cortical circuits in diverse cortical areas of mouse brains has been linked to prediction errors (visual, Keller et al., 2012; Zmarz and Keller, 2016; Fiser et al., 2016; Attinger et al., 2017; Gillon et al., 2021), auditory (Eliades and Wang, 2008; Keller and Hahnloser, 2009), somatosensory (Ayaz et al., 2019), and posterior parietal (Raltschev et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: Prediction errors could be associated with learning.
source: Importantly, prediction errors could be associated with learning (Jordan and Keller, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Prediction error activity results from an imbalance of excitatory and inhibitory inputs.
source: It has been suggested that prediction error activity results from an imbalance of excitatory and inhibitory inputs (Hertäg and Sprekeler, 2020; Hertäg and Clopath, 2022), and that the prediction is subtracted from the sensory input [see e.g. Rao and Ballard, 1999; Attinger et al., 2017], possibly mediated by so-called somatostatin-positive interneurons (SSTs) (Attinger et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical and experimental work.

claim: SSTs possibly mediate the subtraction of prediction from sensory input.
source: It has been suggested that prediction error activity results from an imbalance of excitatory and inhibitory inputs (Hertäg and Sprekeler, 2020; Hertäg and Clopath, 2022), and that the prediction is subtracted from the sensory input [see e.g. Rao and Ballard, 1999; Attinger et al., 2017], possibly mediated by so-called somatostatin-positive interneurons (SSTs) (Attinger et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: One role of inhibition is to modulate the prediction error neuron activity by uncertainty.
source: Here, we hypothesise that one role of inhibition is to modulate the prediction error neuron activity by uncertainty.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Uncertainty should divisively modulate prediction error activity.
source: First, we derive that uncertainty should divisively modulate prediction error activity and introduce uncertainty-modulated prediction errors (UPEs).
evidence: This is derived from normative theory as shown in the Results section.

claim: Layer 2/3 prediction error neurons reflect uncertainty-modulated prediction errors.
source: We hypothesise that, first, layer 2/3 prediction error neurons reflect such UPEs.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Different inhibitory cell types are involved in calculating the difference between predictions and stimuli, and in the uncertainty modulation, respectively.
source: Second, we hypothesise that different inhibitory cell types are involved in calculating the difference between predictions and stimuli, and in the uncertainty modulation, respectively.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: SSTs and PVs play respective roles in subtractive and divisive modulation.
source: Based on experimental findings, we suggest that SSTs and PVs play the respective roles.
evidence: This suggestion is based on experimental findings cited elsewhere in the manuscript.

claim: Single inhibitory cells encode the means and variances of their inputs in a context-dependent manner.
source: Notably, because the information about the stimulus distribution is stored in the connectivity, single inhibitory cells encode the means and variances of their inputs in a context-dependent manner.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the modeling results.

claim: Layer 2/3 pyramidal cells encode uncertainty-modulated prediction errors context-dependently.
source: Layer 2/3 pyramidal cells in this model hence encode uncertainty-modulated prediction errors context-dependently.
evidence: This follows from the model results.

claim: Error neurons can implement out-of-distribution detection by amplifying large errors and reducing small errors with a nonlinear fI-curve.
source: We show that error neurons can additionally implement out-of-distribution detection by amplifying large errors and reducing small errors with a nonlinear fI-curve (activation function).
evidence: This is demonstrated through modeling results shown in Figure 4.

claim: UPEs effectively mediate an adjustable learning rate, which allows fast learning in high-certainty contexts and reduces the learning rate in uncertain contexts.
source: Finally, we demonstrate that UPEs effectively mediate an adjustable learning rate, which allows fast learning in high-certainty contexts and reduces the learning rate, thus suppressing fluctuations in uncertain contexts.
evidence: This is demonstrated through modeling results shown in Figure 7.

claim: Positive and negative prediction errors are represented by distinct neuronal populations.
source: Because baseline firing rates are low in layer 2/3 pyramidal cells [e.g., (Niell and Stryker, 2008)], positive and negative prediction errors were suggested to be represented by distinct neuronal populations (Keller and Mrsic-Flogel, 2018; Rao and Ballard, 1999), which is in line with experimental data (Jordan and Keller, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental and theoretical work.

claim: Layer 2/3 pyramidal cells receive subtractive inhibition from SST and divisive inhibition from PV interneurons.
source: In line with this, prediction error neurons in layer 2/3 receive subtractive inhibition from somatostatin (SST) and divisive inhibition from parvalbumin (PV) interneurons (Wilson et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: SSTs can also have divisive effects, and PVs can have subtractive effects, dependent on circuit and postsynaptic properties.
source: However, SSTs can also have divisive effects, and PVs can have subtractive effects, dependent on circuit and postsynaptic properties (Seybold et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2012; Dorsett et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: After learning, the weight and the average SST firing rate reflect the mean of the presented whisker stimulus intensities.
source: After learning, the weight and the average SST firing rate reflect the mean of the presented whisker stimulus intensities (Figure 2C–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation results shown in Figure 2.

claim: PVs integrate their inputs supralinearly.
source: PVs were shown to integrate their inputs supralinearly (Cornford et al., 2019), which could help PVs to approximately estimate the variance.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: Layer 2/3 pyramidal cells integrate dendritic inputs nonlinearly due to NMDA and calcium spikes.
source: Layer 2/3 pyramidal cell dendrites can generate NMDA and calcium spikes, which cause a nonlinear integration of inputs.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about dendritic properties.

claim: A circuit with prediction error neurons with a dendritic nonlinearity approximates an idealised circuit in which the PV rate perfectly represents the variance.
source: We here show that a circuit with prediction error neurons with a dendritic nonlinearity (as in Figure 4) approximates an idealised circuit, in which the PV rate perfectly represents the variance (Figure 5D and E, see inset for comparison of the two models).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation results shown in Figure 5.

claim: The dendritic nonlinearity can compensate for PV neuron dynamics.
source: The dendritic nonlinearity can hence compensate for PV neuron dynamics.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of model results.

claim: Putative inhibitory neurons in the macaque anterior cingulate cortex increased their firing rates in periods of high uncertainty.
source: First, putative inhibitory neurons (narrow spiking units) in the macaque anterior cingulate cortex increased their firing rates in periods of high uncertainty (Banaie Boroujeni et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: In mice reared in a predictable environment, error neuron responses to mismatches decreased with each day of experiencing unpredictable mismatches.
source: Second, prediction error activity seems to decrease in less predictable, and hence more uncertain, contexts: in mice reared in a predictable environment [where locomotion and visual flow match (Keller et al., 2012)], error neuron responses to mismatches in locomotion and visual flow decreased with each day of experiencing these unpredictable mismatches.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: SST responses decreased during mismatch when visual flow was halted, and there was no difference between mice reared in a predictable or unpredictable environment.
source: In this study, SST responses decreased during mismatch, that is when the visual flow was halted, and there was no difference between mice reared in a predictable or unpredictable environment.
evidence: This refers to experimental results from Attinger et al., 2017.

claim: PV responses were absent towards mismatches in animals reared in an unpredictable environment.
source: In the same study, PV responses were absent towards mismatches in animals reared in an unpredictable environment (Attinger et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: In a low-uncertainty setting, a new mean representation can be learned faster with UPEs in comparison to unmodulated prediction errors.
source: Indeed, in a low-uncertainty setting, a new mean representation can be learned faster with UPEs (in comparison to unmodulated, Figure 7A and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation results shown in Figure 7.

claim: In a high-uncertainty setting, the effective learning rate is smaller, and the mean representation is less variable than in the unmodulated case.
source: In a high-uncertainty setting, the effective learning rate is smaller, and the mean representation is less variable than in the unmodulated case (Figure 7B and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation results shown in Figure 7.

claim: The standard deviation of the firing rate increases only sublinearly with the standard deviation of the inputs.
source: The standard deviation of the firing rate increases only sublinearly with the standard deviation of the inputs (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation results shown in Figure 7.

claim: Uncertainty-modulation of prediction errors enables an adaptive learning rate modulation.
source: In summary, uncertainty-modulation of prediction errors enables an adaptive learning rate modulation.
evidence: This is concluded from the simulation results.

claim: Uncertainty is computed on each level of the hierarchy.
source: We propose that uncertainty is computed on each level of the hierarchy.
evidence: This is a proposal by the authors based on their model.

claim: Multiple neurological disorders, such as autism spectrum disorder or schizophrenia, are associated with maladaptive contextual uncertainty-weighting of sensory and prior information.
source: Multiple neurological disorders, such as autism spectrum disorder or schizophrenia, are associated with maladaptive contextual uncertainty-weighting of sensory and prior information (Goris et al., 2021; Lawson et al., 2014; Van de Cruys et al., 2014; Lawson et al., 2017; Shi et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: ASD is associated with an excitation-inhibition imbalance and reduced inhibition.
source: These disorders are also associated with aberrant inhibition, for example ASD is associated with an excitation-inhibition imbalance (Rubenstein and Merzenich, 2003) and reduced inhibition (Harada et al., 2011; Gaetz et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: PV cells, in particular chandelier PV cells, were shown to be reduced in number and synaptic strength in ASD.
source: Interestingly, PV cells, in particular chandelier PV cells, were shown to be reduced in number and synaptic strength in ASD (Juarez and Martínez Cerdeño, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: PVs have broader sensory tuning than pyramidal cells.
source: The broader sensory tuning of PVs (Cottam et al., 2013) is in line with the model insofar as uncertainty modulation could be more general than the specific feature, which is more likely for low-level features processed in primary sensory cortices.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: PVs connect more to pyramidal cells with similar feature tuning.
source: PVs were shown to connect more to pyramidal cells with similar feature tuning (Znamenskiy et al., 2024) this would be in line with the model, as uncertainty modulation should be feature-related.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: SSTs underlie the effect of surround suppression.
source: SSTs are already known to be involved in spatial prediction, as they underlie the effect of surround suppression (Adesnik et al., 2012), in which SSTs suppress the local activity dependent on a predictive surround.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: There are many different subtypes of SSTs.
source: Indeed, there are many different subtypes of SSTs (Schneider-Mizell et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: SST44 specifically responds when the animal corrects a movement.
source: There is, for example, a type called SST44, which was shown to specifically respond when the animal corrects a movement (Green et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: SSTs receive top-down inputs.
source: SSTs receive top-down inputs (Liu et al., 2020), which could provide the prediction to be subtracted in negative prediction error circuits.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: EI balance has been observed experimentally.
source: Such an EI balance has been observed experimentally (Tan and Wehr, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: Error responses are the result of breaking EI balance.
source: And it has previously been suggested that error responses are the result of breaking this EI balance (Hertäg and Sprekeler, 2020; Barry and Gerstner, 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: Heterosynaptic plasticity is a possible mechanism to achieve EI balance.
source: Heterosynaptic plasticity is a possible mechanism to achieve EI balance (Field et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: Spike pairing in pre- and postsynaptic neurons induces long-term potentiation at co-activated excitatory and inhibitory synapses.
source: For example, spike pairing in pre- and postsynaptic neurons induces long-term potentiation at co-activated excitatory and inhibitory synapses with the degree of inhibitory potentiation depending on the evoked excitation (D'amour and Froemke, 2015), which can normalise EI balance (Field et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental work.
